blocks.content: You join a Zoom call, a Google Meet, or a Discord voice channel, and your camera and microphone reach the other people almost instantly. When you talk, your voice does not take a slow detour through some distant server, it travels as directly as possible to the person you are speaking with.

That direct, low latency media is what WebRTC makes possible. It lets two browsers, or two apps, exchange audio, video, and data directly with each other, peer to peer, without routing every packet through your backend.

It is also the odd one out in this section. Every other technique here connects a client to your server. WebRTC connects one client to another client, and your server mostly just helps them find each other.
That single idea, media between people rather than through a server, changes the cost, the latency, and the whole architecture, which is why WebRTC deserves its own careful look.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278748086-518123290.png
blocks.alt: A signaling server helps two peers meet, then media flows directly between them

blocks.content: 1. What WebRTC Is

WebRTC, which stands for Web Real Time Communication, is a set of browser technologies for real time, peer to peer communication of audio, video, and arbitrary data. It is built into every modern browser, with no plugin required.

The headline capability is direct media between peers. Once two browsers have established a WebRTC connection, their audio and video flow straight between them, taking the shortest path the network allows, which is what makes calls feel live.

It is not only for video. WebRTC can also open a data channel, a peer to peer pipe for any data you like, which is used for things like file sharing, game state, and low latency messaging between users.

["Peer to peer: media and data travel directly between clients","Real time: designed for the lowest possible latency, suitable for live calls","Built into browsers: standard APIs, no plugin or install","Media and data: audio, video, and a general purpose data channel"]
items: Peer to peer: media and data travel directly between clients
Real time: designed for the lowest possible latency, suitable for live calls
Built into browsers: standard APIs, no plugin or install
Media and data: audio, video, and a general purpose data channel

blocks.title: The one line version
blocks.content: WebRTC lets two browsers talk directly to each other, sending audio, video, and data peer to peer with very low latency.
WebRTC came from Google, which open sourced the technology in 2011, and it was then standardised by the W3C and the IETF so every browser could implement the same thing.
It is also what finally replaced browser plugins for real time media. Before WebRTC, video in the browser meant Flash or a custom plugin, and now it is a built in, standard capability.
Because it is a standard, a Chrome user and a Firefox user can join the same call with no extra software, which is a big part of why it became universal.
Today WebRTC is everywhere, from the big video platforms to social audio apps, browser games, and even smart home devices streaming a camera feed.
2. Why WebRTC Is Different
To place WebRTC correctly, contrast it with everything else in this section. Polling, long polling, SSE, and WebSockets all connect a client to your server. The server is always in the middle.

WebRTC breaks that shape. The heavy media stream does not go through your server at all. It goes directly from one user to another. Your server is only involved at the very beginning, to help the two peers discover each other and agree on how to connect.

This matters enormously for cost and latency. Video is huge. If every participant in a call streamed video through your servers, your bandwidth bill and your latency would both explode. By sending media peer to peer, WebRTC keeps that traffic off your infrastructure and takes the shortest network path.

["Client to client, not client to server, for the actual media","Your server only helps peers meet, then steps out of the media path","Low latency, because media takes the direct route between users","Low server cost, because gigabytes of video never touch your backend"]
items: Client to client, not client to server, for the actual media
Your server only helps peers meet, then steps out of the media path
Low latency, because media takes the direct route between users
Low server cost, because gigabytes of video never touch your backend

blocks.title: Where your server still matters
blocks.content: You always need a small server for signaling, the initial introduction between peers. WebRTC deliberately does not define how that happens, so you build it, usually over WebSockets.

A quick bit of math shows the stakes. In a ten person call where everyone sends video, routing all of it through your server means receiving ten streams and sending ninety, an enormous amount of bandwidth per call. Peer to peer, or a smart forwarding server, avoids paying for all of that centrally.
This is the core reason consumer video products could scale at all. The expensive part, the media, mostly stays off the provider infrastructure.
It is also why many teams reach for a managed real time platform, because getting this bandwidth architecture right at scale is a serious undertaking.
3. The Three Core APIs
WebRTC in the browser really comes down to three APIs. Understanding what each one does makes the whole system click.

["getUserMedia: asks the user for camera and microphone access and gives you their media stream","RTCPeerConnection: the heart of WebRTC, it manages the connection to the other peer and carries the media","RTCDataChannel: an optional peer to peer channel for sending arbitrary data, not just media"]
items: getUserMedia: asks the user for camera and microphone access and gives you their media stream
RTCPeerConnection: the heart of WebRTC, it manages the connection to the other peer and carries the media
RTCDataChannel: an optional peer to peer channel for sending arbitrary data, not just media

blocks.content: You start by capturing the local media. This is the line that triggers the browser permission prompt for the camera and microphone.
Then you create a peer connection and add your media to it. The RTCPeerConnection is what actually negotiates and carries the call to the other side.

blocks.title: Notice the iceServers
blocks.content: The RTCPeerConnection is configured with STUN and TURN servers up front. Those are what let it work across the real internet, where peers sit behind routers and firewalls, which we cover soon.
There is also renegotiation. If something changes mid call, such as adding screen sharing to an audio call, the peers create a fresh offer and answer to update the session without tearing it down.
The ontrack callback is how remote media arrives. When the other peer adds a track, your ontrack handler fires with the incoming stream, which you attach to a video element to display it.
These few APIs, capture, connect, and optionally a data channel, are genuinely the whole surface you touch as an application developer. The complexity lives underneath, in connection setup.
Together they turn a browser tab into a full real time media endpoint, something that once required native apps and custom plugins.
4. Connecting Two Peers

Setting up a WebRTC connection is the hardest part to grasp, because the two peers cannot talk to each other yet, so they need a middleman to exchange the setup information. That exchange is called signaling, and the information itself uses a format called SDP.

The core dance is an offer and an answer. One peer creates an offer describing what it wants to send and receive, the other replies with an answer, and alongside this they trade network paths called ICE candidates.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278750894-390003293.png
blocks.alt: Peers trade an SDP offer and answer, plus ICE candidates, through the signaling server

blocks.content: ["Peer A creates an offer, an SDP description of its media, and sends it through signaling","Peer B receives the offer, creates an answer, and sends it back the same way","Both peers gather ICE candidates, the possible network addresses they can be reached at, and exchange them","WebRTC tries the candidate pairs and picks the best working path","Once a path works, media flows directly between the peers"]
items: Peer A creates an offer, an SDP description of its media, and sends it through signaling
Peer B receives the offer, creates an answer, and sends it back the same way
Both peers gather ICE candidates, the possible network addresses they can be reached at, and exchange them
WebRTC tries the candidate pairs and picks the best working path
Once a path works, media flows directly between the peers

blocks.content: The key thing to hold onto is that all of this negotiation goes through your signaling channel, but the moment a path is found, the media leaves that channel and flows directly. Signaling is the introduction, not the conversation.

blocks.title: SDP in one sentence
blocks.content: SDP, the Session Description Protocol, is just a text blob describing what each peer supports, such as codecs and media types. You rarely read it by hand, you just pass it between peers.

In practice ICE candidates are sent as they are discovered, a technique called trickle ICE, rather than waiting to gather them all. This makes connections set up noticeably faster, because peers can start trying paths immediately.
You see this in events like onicecandidate, which fires for each candidate found, and which you forward through signaling to the other peer.
SDP looks intimidating because it is verbose, listing every codec, resolution, and network option, but you almost never edit it. The libraries generate and consume it for you.
5. Signaling: The Part You Build

Here is the point that surprises people most: WebRTC does not include signaling. The specification deliberately leaves out how the offer, answer, and ICE candidates get from one peer to the other. That part is yours to build.

The reason is flexibility. Every application already has its own way of connecting users, so WebRTC lets you carry the setup messages over whatever channel you like. In practice, almost everyone uses WebSockets, because signaling is a two way, real time exchange.

The signaling server itself is small. It does not touch the media. It simply relays messages between the two peers while they negotiate, like a switchboard that connects a call and then gets out of the way.

blocks.title: This is a common interview point
blocks.content: If asked to design a video calling system, state clearly that WebRTC handles the media but you must provide signaling, usually a WebSocket service, plus STUN and TURN servers.
The messages your signaling channel carries are just a few types: an offer, an answer, and a stream of ICE candidates. Your server does not need to understand them, only route them to the right peer.

Signaling also has to scale like any real time service. For many concurrent calls you run a fleet of WebSocket servers, often with a pub sub layer so the two peers of a call can be connected even if they land on different signaling servers.
A neat consequence is reuse. If your app already uses WebSockets for chat, that same channel can carry WebRTC signaling.
6. NAT Traversal: STUN and TURN

There is a hard problem hiding under all of this. Most devices do not have a public internet address. They sit behind a home router or a company firewall that performs NAT, network address translation. So peer A cannot simply send packets to peer B, because it does not know a reachable address for B, and B is hidden behind its router.
WebRTC solves this with two kinds of helper servers, STUN and TURN.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278752814-815451290.png
blocks.alt: STUN helps a peer learn its public address; TURN relays media when a direct path is impossible

blocks.content: ["STUN: a lightweight server that tells a peer what its public address looks like from the outside, so the two peers can try to connect directly through their NATs","TURN: a relay server that sits in the middle and forwards media when a direct connection is impossible, for example behind strict corporate firewalls","ICE: the framework that gathers all the candidate addresses and systematically finds a pair that works"]
items: STUN: a lightweight server that tells a peer what its public address looks like from the outside, so the two peers can try to connect directly through their NATs
TURN: a relay server that sits in the middle and forwards media when a direct connection is impossible, for example behind strict corporate firewalls
ICE: the framework that gathers all the candidate addresses and systematically finds a pair that works

blocks.content: The order of preference is direct first, relay last. WebRTC always tries to connect the peers directly, using STUN to discover addresses. Only when every direct path fails does it fall back to relaying through TURN.

blocks.title: TURN is not free
blocks.content: When a call falls back to TURN, the media does flow through your server after all, so you pay for that bandwidth. A meaningful fraction of real world calls, often around ten to twenty percent, need TURN, so you must budget for it.

ICE gathers several kinds of candidate address. A host candidate is the device local address, a server reflexive candidate is the public address discovered through STUN, and a relay candidate is an address on a TURN server. ICE tries them in order of preference, direct before relayed.
The hardest case is a symmetric NAT, a strict router that makes a direct connection nearly impossible. When both peers sit behind such NATs, relaying through TURN is often the only thing that works.
This is why you cannot skip TURN in production. Your demo on one network works with STUN alone, but real users on strict corporate or mobile networks need the relay to connect at all.
TURN can even relay over TCP on port 443 to slip through firewalls that block everything except web traffic, which is the last resort that makes calls connect almost anywhere.
7. The Connection Lifecycle
An RTCPeerConnection moves through a series of states, and watching them is how you know whether a call is healthy. This is a genuine state machine, not a simple linear flow.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028628-544081300.png
blocks.alt: The RTCPeerConnection connection state machine, from new through connected to closed

blocks.content: ["New: the connection is created but not yet started","Connecting: ICE is trying candidate paths to reach the other peer","Connected: a path succeeded and media is flowing","Disconnected: connectivity was lost, often a temporary network blip","Failed: no path could be established or recovered, the call cannot continue","Closed: the connection was intentionally ended"]
items: New: the connection is created but not yet started
Connecting: ICE is trying candidate paths to reach the other peer
Connected: a path succeeded and media is flowing
Disconnected: connectivity was lost, often a temporary network blip
Failed: no path could be established or recovered, the call cannot continue
Closed: the connection was intentionally ended

blocks.content: The important transitions are the recovery ones. A brief network change can drop the connection to disconnected, and WebRTC will often recover back to connected on its own. If it cannot, it moves to failed, and your application should surface that and try to reconnect or renegotiate.

blocks.title: Handle the sad states
blocks.content: A robust call app listens for the disconnected and failed states and reacts, showing a reconnecting indicator or restarting ICE. Assuming a connection stays healthy forever is a common bug.

There are actually two related state properties worth watching. iceConnectionState reflects the ICE path status specifically, while connectionState is the overall summary. You watch connectionState for the big picture and iceConnectionState when debugging connectivity.

When a connection degrades, one recovery tool is an ICE restart, which re gathers candidates and finds a fresh path without rebuilding the whole call. It is the standard way to recover from a network change like switching from Wi Fi to mobile data.
Surfacing state to the user matters too. A small reconnecting indicator during a disconnected state reassures people, rather than leaving them staring at a frozen video.
8. Media: Tracks, Codecs, and Quality
The media itself is organised into tracks. A typical call has an audio track and a video track, and each is added to the peer connection and sent to the other side.

Before media flows, the peers must agree on a codec, the format used to compress audio and video. This agreement happens during the offer and answer. Common video codecs are VP8, VP9, and H.264, and a common audio codec is Opus. If two peers share no codec, they cannot exchange that kind of media.

WebRTC also adapts to the network in real time. If bandwidth drops or packets are lost, it lowers the video bitrate and resolution to keep the call going, and raises them again when conditions improve. This is why a call gets blurry for a moment on a weak connection rather than freezing entirely.

["Tracks: separate streams for audio and video, added to the connection","Codecs: the compression formats peers must agree on, like Opus for audio and VP8 or H.264 for video","Adaptive bitrate: quality is turned down and up automatically as the network changes","Built for loss: WebRTC uses UDP under the hood and tolerates some packet loss to stay real time"]
items: Tracks: separate streams for audio and video, added to the connection
Codecs: the compression formats peers must agree on, like Opus for audio and VP8 or H.264 for video
Adaptive bitrate: quality is turned down and up automatically as the network changes
Built for loss: WebRTC uses UDP under the hood and tolerates some packet loss to stay real time

blocks.title: Why UDP, not TCP
blocks.content: Media rides on UDP because for a live call, a slightly dropped frame is better than waiting for a retransmission. Being a little lossy but always current is exactly right for real time audio and video.

A powerful trick in modern calls is simulcast, where a sender encodes its video at several resolutions at once and sends all of them. A forwarding server can then give each receiver the quality its network can handle.
Under the hood, WebRTC constantly estimates the available bandwidth and feeds that back to the encoder, which is what drives the automatic quality changes you see.
A small jitter buffer on the receiver smooths out packets that arrive late or out of order, trading a few milliseconds of delay for a steadier picture and clearer audio.
The Opus audio codec is worth a mention, since it adapts its own bitrate and handles packet loss gracefully, a big reason WebRTC voice sounds good even on shaky connections.
9. Data Channels
WebRTC is not only about media. The RTCDataChannel gives you a peer to peer pipe for sending any data directly between users, with the same low latency as the media path.
Once the peer connection is set up, opening a data channel is simple, and it behaves a lot like a WebSocket, except the messages travel directly between the two clients instead of through a server.

["Peer to peer: data goes directly between users, not via your server","Configurable: you can choose reliable and ordered, like TCP, or fast and lossy, like UDP","Low latency: it shares the same optimised path as the media","Use cases: file transfer, multiplayer game state, chat, and collaborative tools"]
items: Peer to peer: data goes directly between users, not via your server
Configurable: you can choose reliable and ordered, like TCP, or fast and lossy, like UDP
Low latency: it shares the same optimised path as the media
Use cases: file transfer, multiplayer game state, chat, and collaborative tools

blocks.content: This is what powers peer to peer file sharing in the browser and the snappy, direct interactions in some multiplayer games and collaborative apps.
Data channels are built on SCTP, which runs over the same secure peer connection as the media, which is why they inherit the low latency path and the mandatory encryption.

You can tune reliability per channel. A file transfer wants reliable, ordered delivery like TCP, while a stream of game position updates is better off fast and lossy, where the newest update simply replaces the last.
10. Multi-party: Mesh, SFU, and MCU
Peer to peer is wonderful for two people, but calls with many participants force a real architectural choice, because pure peer to peer does not scale.

In a mesh, every participant connects directly to every other participant. For three people it is fine, but the connections grow quadratically, and each person must upload their video to everyone. By five or six participants, most devices cannot keep up.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028627-248463762.png
blocks.alt: Mesh: every peer connects to every other, so connections and uploads explode

blocks.content: The usual fix is an SFU, a Selective Forwarding Unit. Each participant sends their stream once to the SFU, and the SFU forwards it to everyone else. Uploads stay constant, and the server does cheap forwarding rather than heavy processing.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278758104-562395483.png
blocks.alt: SFU: each peer uploads once to a server that forwards the stream to the others

blocks.content: An MCU, a Multipoint Control Unit, goes further and mixes all the streams into a single combined stream. This is easiest on the participants, since each receives just one stream, but it is expensive on the server because mixing video is heavy work.

{"headers":["Approach","How it works","Scales to","Server cost"],"rows":[["Mesh","Everyone connects to everyone","A few people","None, but heavy on clients"],["SFU","Each sends once, server forwards","Dozens","Moderate, mostly bandwidth"],["MCU","Server mixes into one stream","Large calls","High, heavy processing"]]}
Most real group calling products, like large meetings, use an SFU, because it balances client load and server cost well. This is exactly the kind of tradeoff to name in an interview.

SFUs get smarter with simulcast. Because each sender provides several quality layers, the SFU can forward a high layer to a viewer on fast internet and a low layer to one on a phone, all without decoding or re encoding.

MCUs still have their place, for example when a client is too limited to handle many streams, or when you need a single recorded or broadcast output, since the server already produces one combined stream.
The rule of thumb people use is mesh for up to about three or four participants, and an SFU beyond that, which covers the vast majority of real applications.
11. Security
WebRTC is encrypted by default, and this is not optional. There is no way to send unencrypted media, which is a strong and deliberate design choice.

["Media is encrypted with SRTP, the secure form of the real time transport protocol","The keys are negotiated with DTLS, the datagram form of TLS","The browser requires user permission before the camera or microphone can be accessed","Signaling should run over a secure channel, such as WebSockets over TLS, since it carries connection setup"]
items: Media is encrypted with SRTP, the secure form of the real time transport protocol
The keys are negotiated with DTLS, the datagram form of TLS
The browser requires user permission before the camera or microphone can be accessed
Signaling should run over a secure channel, such as WebSockets over TLS, since it carries connection setup

blocks.content: The one part you must secure yourself is signaling, because WebRTC does not define it. If an attacker can inject messages into your signaling channel, they could interfere with call setup, so authenticate and encrypt it like any sensitive endpoint.

blocks.title: Encrypted end to end by path, not always by content
blocks.content: In a direct peer to peer call the media is effectively end to end encrypted. With an SFU the server forwards encrypted packets without decoding them, but true end to end encryption across an SFU needs extra techniques, which is worth knowing if privacy is a requirement.
The encryption is set up with a DTLS handshake between the peers as the connection forms, which exchanges the keys later used by SRTP to protect every media packet.

For true end to end encryption through an SFU, browsers support insertable streams, which let the application encrypt media so even the forwarding server cannot read it. This is how privacy focused calling apps protect media across a server.
12. When to Use WebRTC
WebRTC is the right tool for a specific shape of problem: real time, peer to peer media or data with the lowest possible latency.

["Video and voice calls, one to one or in groups","Live audio, such as social audio rooms","Screen sharing and remote control","Peer to peer file transfer directly between browsers","Low latency multiplayer game data over data channels"]
items: Video and voice calls, one to one or in groups
Live audio, such as social audio rooms
Screen sharing and remote control
Peer to peer file transfer directly between browsers
Low latency multiplayer game data over data channels

blocks.content: It is the wrong tool for most other real time needs. If you only need to push updates from a server to a browser, SSE or WebSockets are far simpler. WebRTC brings signaling, STUN, TURN, and NAT traversal, which is a lot of machinery to take on if you do not actually need direct peer to peer media.
Use WebRTC when users need to exchange audio, video, or low latency data directly with each other. For server to client updates, reach for SSE or WebSockets instead.

The set of good fits is wider than just calls. Screen sharing, remote desktop and support tools, cloud gaming input, drone and robot control, and browser based file sharing all use WebRTC for its direct, low latency path.
The common thread is always the same: two endpoints that need to exchange a lot of data, or very timely data, directly and with minimal delay.
If in doubt, ask whether the media truly needs to go peer to peer. If a server in the middle is fine, a simpler transport usually is too.
13. Common Challenges and Mistakes
WebRTC is powerful but famously fiddly, and the difficulties cluster in a few predictable places.

["Forgetting TURN, so calls work on your office network but fail for users behind strict firewalls","Underestimating signaling, treating it as an afterthought when it is a real service you must build and secure","Trying to use a mesh for large calls, which overwhelms client devices, when an SFU is needed","Not handling the disconnected and failed states, so calls silently die instead of reconnecting","Ignoring TURN bandwidth cost, which can be a significant part of the bill for relayed calls"]
items: Forgetting TURN, so calls work on your office network but fail for users behind strict firewalls
Underestimating signaling, treating it as an afterthought when it is a real service you must build and secure
Trying to use a mesh for large calls, which overwhelms client devices, when an SFU is needed
Not handling the disconnected and failed states, so calls silently die instead of reconnecting
Ignoring TURN bandwidth cost, which can be a significant part of the bill for relayed calls

blocks.content: The through line is that the happy path, two people on good networks, is easy, and everything hard about WebRTC is about the real world: NATs, firewalls, flaky networks, and scaling beyond two people.

blocks.title: Consider a managed service
blocks.content: Because operating STUN, TURN, and SFU infrastructure is genuinely hard, many teams use a managed WebRTC platform that provides them, and focus their own effort on the application.

For debugging, the browser gives you real tools. In Chrome, the page chrome://webrtc-internals shows every active connection, its state, and detailed statistics, which is invaluable when a call misbehaves.

Programmatically, the getStats method on a peer connection reports live metrics like bitrate, packet loss, and round trip time, which production apps use to show call quality indicators and to diagnose issues.
Cross browser quirks still exist despite standardisation, so real applications lean on a wrapper library like adapter.js to smooth over the differences between browsers.
Mobile networks are the real stress test, since a phone can switch from Wi Fi to cellular mid call, change its address, and force an ICE restart, all of which a robust app must handle smoothly.
14. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This
blocks.text: 14. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This

blocks.content: When a design involves live video, voice, or direct peer to peer data, WebRTC is the answer, and the interviewer wants to see that you understand the pieces around the media.
Frame the shape: I explain that WebRTC carries media directly between peers, so my server only handles signaling and does not sit in the media path.
Name the supporting cast: I always mention that I need a signaling service, usually WebSockets, plus STUN for address discovery and TURN as a relay fallback.
Choose the topology: For two people I use direct peer to peer, and for group calls I use an SFU, because a mesh does not scale past a handful of participants.
Budget for reality: I call out that a share of calls will need TURN relay, which costs bandwidth, and that I must handle failed and disconnected states for flaky networks.

Right size the effort: I note that building STUN, TURN, and an SFU is a large undertaking, so unless real time media is core to the product, I would use a managed WebRTC platform and focus on the application itself.
